Summable smoothing and fixed Fourier tests

Written by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), October 2026. Public domain (CC0).

Directional regularity is usually tested by compact distributions that depend on the derivative order. A nonquasianalytic class admits a simpler test: one compact distribution works at every order. The mechanism is a compact cutoff in the same class. We construct such cutoffs, quantify their derivatives in an arbitrary finite-dimensional norm, and prove the fixed-distribution criterion.

The earlier derivative-growth lesson, Lemma 1, Proposition 2 and Theorem 6, proves the fixed-index estimates, algebra properties and full-frequency Fourier criterion. Cones and derivative-growth wavefronts, Lemma 2 and Theorems 3–4, proves the exact conic localization estimates used below. Compactness and continuous extrema have the proofs in the scalar foundation, Sections 12.5–12.7; its Section 13.4 gives the fundamental theorem of calculus. Product integration, domination and affine substitution are proved in the integration foundation, Sections 15.0–15.1 and 16.1–16.2.

The finite algebra foundation, Section 10, supplies bases and the alternating determinant identities. We use ordinary derivatives, the Fourier phase , and the admissible scales

Lemma 2 (a norm-adapted basis). In a real normed space of dimension , there is a basis , with coordinate functionals , for which

Proof. Start with any basis. The triangle inequality bounds the given norm by a constant times the Euclidean coordinate norm and makes it continuous in those coordinates. Its minimum on the Euclidean unit sphere is positive, by compactness, continuity and positivity of a norm. Hence its closed unit ball is compact in these same coordinates. On the product of such balls, maximize the absolute coordinate determinant. The maximum is positive because some scaled basis lies in the balls. A maximizing tuple is a basis, and every member has norm one: otherwise increasing that vector to norm one increases the determinant. Replacing its -th column by any unit-ball vector multiplies the determinant by . Maximality gives ; scaling gives the first inequality for every . The expansion and the triangle inequality give the rest. This uses the finite determinant identity, not an ellipsoid comparison.

Flat functions and compact cutoffs

A class is quasianalytic in one dimension if a member on any connected open interval whose derivatives of every order vanish at one point vanishes throughout that interval. It is nonquasianalytic if this implication fails. This definition refers to uniqueness from an infinite jet; it does not assert that a Taylor series converges.

Exercise 3 (why the analytic full-frequency test needs sequences). Put for , and let near zero. Show that no , equal to there, can satisfy (S14) in all nonzero frequency directions. Explain why this does not contradict analytic regularity of .

Solution. If it did, the constant sequence would meet the full-frequency criterion of Theorem 6 in the derivative-growth lesson. Hence , regarded as a distribution on , would be represented locally everywhere by a function, with the local representatives agreeing because their distributions agree. Its Proposition 3 identifies the scale with the analytic class; for shows that the scale here gives the same class. The resulting analytic function is zero off the compact support and is therefore identically zero by the analytic identity argument proved in its Exercise 2. This contradicts near zero. The original definition allows a bounded sequence whose high derivatives grow with ; the cutoff and Fourier characterization in that lesson apply to the analytic function . There is no claim here that a fixed witness fails on every individual cone for every analytic distribution.
